title: They trade child sex abuse material. They find each other on TikTok
gist: Investigative journalist Katherine Denkinson uncovered 176 TikTok accounts with over two million combined followers that used AI-generated imagery and repurposed videos of real children to signpost Telegram channels trading and selling child sexual abuse material. TikTok's in-app reporting repeatedly found no rule violations until the press approached it, and the author argues current UK law (Online Safety Act, under-16 ban) is insufficient and platforms should be barred from monetising content featuring under-18s and sanctioned for safeguarding failures.

insights.claim: An investigation identified 176 TikTok accounts with more than two million followers between them that manipulated TikTok's safeguarding systems to advertise Telegram channels where child sexual abuse material is traded and sold.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Exposes material content-moderation failure at TikTok, raising regulatory, legal and reputational risk.
insights.quote: This was only one of 176 TikTok accounts that I would eventually uncover.
insights.locator: Visiting those channels, which were public

insights.claim: The accounts used four signalling methods: misappropriated videos of real children, cartoonish AI-generated videos of children, realistic AI videos of children, and AI-generated images of convicted child abusers.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Generative AI is being used to evade automated moderation, a growing cost and liability vector for platforms.
insights.locator: So how are these TikTokers getting around

insights.claim: Thirteen accounts posting AI-generated content of children, based in Russia, Spain and Australia, had more than 50,000 followers, and 15 East Asian accounts with over 50,000 followers used videos to lure viewers onto Telegram channels selling material involving real children.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Cross-border operation complicates enforcement and highlights Telegram's role as a distribution hub.

insights.claim: The investigator found that TikTok's recommendation algorithm surfaced this content after three days of viewing 'edgy' dark-web videos, and later shifted from AI imagery to videos of real children.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Recommendation algorithms actively route users toward harmful networks, strengthening the case for algorithmic liability.

insights.claim: Via open-source investigation the author identified 45 men in 28 countries, aged mid-twenties to mid-eighties and spanning a broad social cross-section, commenting sexually on children's videos and engaging with CSAM-promoting accounts.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Shows the scale and normality of offending users, undermining the 'fringe' defence of platforms.
insights.locator: Commenters on other videos I came across

insights.claim: TikTok's in-app system returned the author's reports as not violating any rules or laws, sometimes offering only to hide content from UK users, even though both AI-generated and real-child CSAM are illegal in the UK.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Geo-hiding rather than removal suggests compliance-minimal moderation that may not satisfy the Online Safety Act.
insights.quote: my reports, made via the platform, were returned with a message to say that they had violated neither

insights.claim: TikTok, Facebook and Instagram all told the author that accounts of identified men, including registered sex offenders, had not broken any rules.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Moderation gaps extend across Meta platforms too, implying sector-wide regulatory exposure.
insights.locator: A search via the Megan’s Law website

insights.claim: TikTok says it removes 99 per cent of violative videos before they are viewed and reports cases to NCMEC, yet all the accounts its in-app system failed to flag were removed only after the journalist approached it for comment.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Gap between claimed and observed enforcement is the kind of evidence regulators use to justify fines.
insights.quote: We invest in advanced moderation technologies, which help us take down 99 per cent of violative videos before they are ever viewed

insights.claim: The Home Office says platforms must proactively identify and remove CSAM under the Online Safety Act, that Ofcom is already investigating Telegram, and that under the Crime and Policing Act those who run such sites face up to 10 years in prison.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Active Ofcom investigation of Telegram signals enforcement risk for messaging platforms in the UK.
insights.locator: When I asked the Home Office

insights.claim: Most of the 176 accounts used videos of real children, downloaded from innocent posts by parents or the children themselves, then recaptioned and reposted them.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Parent-generated child content is a key input to abuse networks, putting the child-influencer economy under scrutiny.

insights.claim: Successful child-influencer accounts can have millions of followers and earn hundreds of thousands of pounds through brand partnerships and monetisation.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: A sizeable creator-economy segment is exposed to potential monetisation bans on under-18 content.
insights.quote: successful child-influencer accounts have millions of followers and can make hundreds of thousands of pounds through brand partnerships and monetisation

insights.claim: Parents' only current protections are blocking users or making accounts private, which limits reach and monetisation and so disincentivises many from doing so.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Platform monetisation incentives work against child safety, a structural conflict regulators may target.
insights.locator: Currently, the only way to prevent

insights.claim: The UK government confirmed in June 2026 that under-16s will be banned from certain social media from spring 2027, but this does not stop parents posting content of their children.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: The under-16 ban will reduce youth user bases on UK social platforms from 2027.

insights.claim: Denkinson argues the Online Safety Act and the under-16 social media ban are clearly insufficient to tackle CSAM proliferation on platforms like TikTok.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Points toward further UK platform legislation beyond current rules.
insights.locator: The existing legislation against online harms

insights.claim: The author proposes legislation preventing platforms from monetising content featuring under-18s, plus sanctions when safeguarding measures are easily bypassed or automated systems fail to detect threats.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: A ban on monetising under-18 content would hit creator payouts and ad revenue tied to family content.
insights.quote: To create a law which prevents platforms from monetising content featuring under-18s would lessen the appeal of “children as content”

insights.claim: Royal Holloway's Derek Perkins says the National Crime Agency is aware of this threat, with its major concern being the number of 14- to 20-year-old males drawn into CSAM, animal cruelty and self-harm content.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
insights.so_what: Law enforcement focus on young male radicalisation online may drive new platform obligations.
insights.locator: The network uncovered in this investigation

insights.claim: Experts quoted, including the National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children's Rani Govender, say ultimate responsibility for these harms lies with the platforms rather than parents.
insights.speaker: Katherine Denkinson
entities: National Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Children
insights.so_what: Policy consensus is shifting liability onto platforms, raising compliance costs.
